title: Sales Enablement Playbook — Positioning, Competitive Briefs, Pitch Decks, Pricing Guidance, Case Studies, Security FAQ
author: Ayesha Patel
summary: Unified sales enablement playbook for Redwood Inference covering core positioning and messaging, competitor battlecards, pitch deck guidance, pricing guardrails, short customer case studies, and a prospect-facing security FAQ.
content:
Overview

Purpose:
- Provide field teams (AE, SDR, SE) with a single reference for positioning Redwood Inference in discovery and demos.
- Equip reps with competitive talking points, a repeatable pitch-deck outline and speaker notes, pricing guardrails, short customer case studies, and a prospect security FAQ.

Target audience (ICP):
- AI-native startups (PLG + engineering-led adoption) looking to optimize inference economics.
- Mid-market product teams that require predictable latency and data controls.
- Enterprise platform and security teams evaluating dedicated or private deployments.

Core value props (one-liners):
- For engineering teams: "Redwood Inference gives you consistent, production-grade LLM inference with predictable latency and unit economics across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments."
- For platform leads: "A single runtime and tooling surface that standardizes inference across apps and environments, reducing ops overhead and cost drift."

Key positioning pillars (talking tracks):
1) Production-first reliability and observability:
   - Emphasize SLO-ready features: per-route latency dashboards, token-level cost attribution, tracing hooks, and automatic fallbacks to model variants.
   - Example talking line: "We instrument token-level costs and provide per-route dashboards so you can catch regressions before they hit users."
2) Economic control and performance levers:
   - Highlight batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization profiles, and smart routing as levers to lower per-token cost without reengineering prompts.
   - Example metric: "Customers typically see a 30-50% reduction in per-token cost after enabling cache+batching recommendations."
3) Flexible deployment modes:
   - Hosted API for fast POC and scale. Dedicated for committed throughput and isolation. Private/VPC or on-prem for regulated workloads and audit requirements.
   - Positioning line: "Same API, same tooling — pick the deployment model that matches your security and latency needs."
4) Developer ergonomics and model lifecycle:
   - Model catalog, version pinning, canary rollouts, and built-in eval hooks for quality regression detection.

Competitive brief (battlecard) — quick reference:
- Competitors covered: OpenAI, Anthropic, Cloud-managed endpoints (AWS SageMaker / Google Vertex), Self-hosted inference vendors (open source runtimes + orchestration).
- High-level differentiation table: (use in calls as a quick script)
   - OpenAI / Large LLM vendors:
     - Strengths: broad model capabilities, brand recognition, fast innovation cadence.
     - Weaknesses: limited deployment isolation, less transparency into unit economics, fewer on-prem/private options.
     - Redwood rebuttal: "If you need predictable latency, cost controls, and private deployment options for regulated data, Redwood provides the control plane and runtime optimizations to make that feasible at scale."
   - Anthropic / Safety-focused model providers:
     - Strengths: focused model safety and instruction tuning.
     - Weaknesses: similar to OpenAI on isolation; fewer ops controls and observability for production inference.
     - Redwood rebuttal: "You can pair Redwood with curated/open models, apply quantization and caching, and keep the safety tooling you need while gaining operational control."
   - Cloud-managed endpoints (SageMaker / Vertex AI):
     - Strengths: deep cloud integration and broad infra services.
     - Weaknesses: heavier ops footprint, inconsistent performance across instance types, limited model-level rollout tooling.
     - Redwood rebuttal: "Our managed hosting + Dedicated options give you cloud-scale with inference-first optimizations and lower engineering overhead for model rollouts and cost management."
   - Self-hosted runtimes / OSS stacks:
     - Strengths: maximum control, low-level customization.
     - Weaknesses: team build/ops cost, slower iteration, lack of integrated observability and SLAs.
     - Redwood rebuttal: "We combine a proven serving runtime with a control plane and observability built for production, lowering total cost of ownership compared to DIY."

Battlecard quick scripts (for objections):
- "We already use OpenAI / another managed provider" → "What are you seeing on variance in latency and per-token cost? We help teams reduce cost and smooth latency through batching + caching while offering private deployment for compliance."
- "We will self-host to control cost" → "Many teams undercount build/ops and struggle to maintain SLOs. Redwood offloads that investment while still providing isolation and KMS integration for keys."

Pitch deck outline + speaker notes (6-8 slides recommended for discovery calls):
1) Title / Hook (1 slide)
   - Hook: latency, cost, and reliability are the hidden engineering tax for LLMs.
   - Speaker note: "Open with customer pain: a failed demo caused by token throttling + unpredictable costs."
2) Market and problem (1 slide)
   - Data point: growing open model ecosystem and rising inference spend.
   - Speaker note: "Emphasize that model choice no longer differentiates teams — serving does."
3) Redwood value proposition (1 slide)
   - Short bullets: unified runtime, predictable economics, flexible deployment.
   - Speaker note: "Map to the buyer persona: platform = standardization, security = private deploy, engineering = latency/cost."
4) How it works (1 slide)
   - Illustration: Serving runtime + smart routing + cache/batching + control plane.
   - Speaker note: "Keep technical but high-level; call out quantization profiles and KV cache."
5) Pricing and commitment options (1 slide)
   - Hosted usage-based vs Dedicated reserved capacity vs Private licensing.
   - Speaker note: "Walk through a sample calculation we keep in the playbook."
6) Case studies / proof (1 slide)
   - Two short bullets with metrics.
   - Speaker note: "Use the short case studies below; swap to the relevant one for the prospect's vertical."
7) Security & compliance (1 slide)
   - Controls: SOC 2, VPC, KMS/HSM, audit logs, data residency options.
   - Speaker note: "Offer to connect prospect with solutions architect and security PM."
8) Next steps / ask (1 slide)
   - Options: 1-week POC, Capacity sizing workshop, Security review.

Pricing guidance — guardrails and examples (rules of thumb for AEs/SEs):
- Pricing models available:
  - Hosted (usage-based): per-token generation + per-embedding rates; discounts at volume tiers.
  - Dedicated (reserved capacity): monthly commit with burst options; predictable throughput and SLA.
  - Private (enterprise license): platform fee + deployment/support contract.
- Example guardrail calculations (illustrative, use quoting tool for official numbers):
  - Example A (POC, low volume): Hosted API, expect $X–$Y/mo (use credits) — emphasize time-to-value.
  - Example B (growth production, 5M tokens/day): Dedicated with reserved GPU pool often reduces unit cost by 30-45% vs hosted list rates.
  - Example C (regulated, high-throughput): Private deployment; total cost includes infra + platform fee; highlight value of SLAs and reduced ops headcount.
- Discounting rules (field guidance):
  - Standard enterprise discounts apply on committed spend; engage sales ops for >12 month or >$200k ARR deals.
  - Avoid unilateral deep discounting to protect margins on dedicated capacity where utilization matters.

Short case studies (swap into pitch where relevant):
1) Kaizen Commerce — AI-native personalization (Hosted -> Dedicated)
   - Problem: Erratic latency and high per-session inference spend during holiday spike.
   - Solution: Began on Hosted API for fast integration; moved to Dedicated reserved pool with autoscaling and caching.
   - Outcome: 42% reduction in per-token cost, 3x reduction in 95th percentile latency, and consistent throughput during peak.
   - Relevant features: Redwood API, Dedicated reserved capacity, automatic KV caching, per-route dashboards.
2) FinSecure — Regulated financial product (Private)
   - Problem: Data residency and audit requirements; internal risk teams insisted on private deployment and KMS control.
   - Solution: Private VPC deployment with KMS integration and audit logging; rollout via canary and A/B quality checks.
   - Outcome: Achieved internal compliance sign-off, maintained latency SLO (95th < 250ms for short queries), and reduced ops burden compared to building an in-house runtime.
   - Relevant features: Private deployment, KMS/HSM, audit logs, rollout policies.

Security FAQ for prospects (top questions and recommended answers):
Q: What certifications and third-party audits does Redwood have?
A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and is working toward ISO 27001. We share an SOC 2 report under NDA and provide audit artifacts to enterprise customers during procurement.

Q: How is customer data isolated and encrypted?
A: Data is encrypted at rest and in transit. For Dedicated and Private, customers can optionally bring keys via KMS/HSM. We support per-tenant isolation at the control plane and data plane for Dedicated pools.

Q: Can we run Redwood in our VPC or on-prem?
A: Yes — Private deployment options include VPC-hosted control plane and an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. Solutions engineering supports sizing and deployment.

Q: Do you retain logs or model inputs?
A: Default retention follows our data-retention policy; customers can opt-in or opt-out of usage retention. Enterprise Private customers can also configure local-only logging. We provide audit logs for all admin actions.

Q: How are keys and secrets managed?
A: We integrate with major KMS providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and support customer-managed keys for private deployments.

Q: What controls exist to prevent model quality/regression drift in production?
A: Redwood provides built-in eval hooks, alerting on regression against saved prompt sets, per-route quality metrics, and canary/A-B rollout tooling to reduce blast radius.

Sales operational checklist (pre-demo / pre-procurement):
1) Identify persona and ICP fit: product/platform/engineering/security.
2) Ask: current inference spend, latency pain points, regulatory constraints.
3) Recommend deployment path: Hosted POC vs Dedicated sizing workshop vs Private security review.
4) Prepare: relevant case study, security docs (SOC 2), and baseline pricing estimate.
5) Offer next-step options: 1-week POC, capacity workshop, or technical deep-dive with SE + Solutions Engineer.

Assets and playbook maintenance:
- Canonical assets (links): pitch-deck template, pricing calculator, SOC 2 redacted report (NDA), dedicated sizing worksheet, case study one-pagers.
- Ownership: go-to-market owns content; SE team maintains tech details. Update cadence: quarterly or when new product features change positioning (e.g., new dedicated SKU, quantization profile release).

Appendix — useful talking metrics and internal product names:
- Product names to reference: Redwood API (hosted), Redwood Dedicated, Redwood Private, Redwood Console, Redwood Optimize.
- Common SLO targets cited in sales conversations: 95th percentile latency goals (hosted: <600ms typical; dedicated: <250ms for short sequences depending on model/hardware).
- Typical uplift claims (non-guaranteed): 30-50% cost reduction from batching + caching + quantization; 2-4x improvement in tail latency with Dedicated pools and kernel selection.
